keeps.text: Let's talk about the summer of 1855 and a decision made by the US Army that nobody at the fort could quite explain.
The Army sent men clear across the Pacific Ocean. They came back to Texas with 33 animals
and 3 handlers who were the only ones who knew how to manage these animals.
Why would they do such a thing?
Well, out west, the army had a big problem.
They had to haul supplies across harsh country that would chew up horses and spit out the bones.
Horses were valuable, and the army wasn't willing to bet a whole supply train of them that they would survive the harsh journey.
So they got creative.
Pull up a chair. This is Old West Stories, and this one is gonna be good.
In 1857, Edward Beale got his orders. He was to survey a wagon road west from what is now northeastern Arizona all the way to Southern California.
along with that assignment came an instruction that raised a few eyebrows on the frontier.
The Army handed Beale 25 unusual animals and told him to see if they could haul road-building supplies across harsh country that horses, mules, and oxen previously didn't survive.
Beale set out, not sure what to expect from these critters. Truth be told, he didn't know much about caring for them either. It's a good thing those 3 handlers came along.
Up ahead lay the Jornada del Muerto,
In Spanish, that means "the journey of the dead man," and the name certainly fit.
It was roughly 90 miles of desert with very little water, where countless people and livestock had perished before.
To Beale's amazement, these strange animals crossed the Jornada del Muerto without a lick of trouble.
By December, the expedition was pulling into Los Angeles, and the animals drew their fair share of attention.
Folks lined the streets to get a good look.
Newspapers ran stories. Those critters were the talk of the territory and the star of the show.
Then trouble came.
Beale made his way back to Camp Verde, the Texas post where the whole venture had started.
Before long, the Civil War reached Texas and Camp Verde fell into Confederate hands, and they had no idea what to do with the animals.
Most were auctioned off.
Some went to zoos. Some went to circuses.
Others simply walked away.
And here's the part of the story that you won't find in the history books.
As late as the early 1900s, Folks were still spotting strange wandering creatures from Arkansas all the way to Mexico.
Plenty of folks swore they'd seen one with their own eyes,
and a fair number of those sightings traced back to Beale's expedition
over 40 years before.
You see,
Beale couldn't cross that harsh Southwest with horses and mules,
so the Army gave him
Camels.
Now, if you came across a wild camel roaming the Arizona desert today, what would you do? Drop your answer in the comments below.
Like, share, and subscribe, and we'll see you in the next story.
